---
title: "MetaVidence tutorials"
---

MetaVidence does meta-analysis without code. You load a spreadsheet, choose the
parameters and get publication-ready plots and tables, all in the browser, with
nothing to install and without your data leaving your computer.

## Where to start

1. **[Get started](get-started.qmd)** shows how to open MetaVidence in the
   browser, and how to install R, RStudio and the package if you would rather
   run it on your own computer.
2. **[The three-step flow](flow.qmd)** walks the screens end to end: data,
   parameters and export. Every module works this way.
3. **Your module's page** covers only what changes in it, such as the required
   columns and the summary measure.

Every module ships an example dataset with 12 studies. It is worth running the
analysis on it before using your own data, so you can see what each screen
produces without preparing a spreadsheet.

## Choosing the module

| You have… | Use |
|---|---|
| Event counts and sample sizes in both groups | [Binary outcomes](binary.qmd) |
| Mean and SD, median and IQR, or a mix of the two | [Continuous outcomes](continuous.qmd) |
| The effect already calculated, with CI or standard error | [Pre-calculated effects](precalculated.qmd) |
| One proportion or mean per study, no comparison | [Single arm](single-arm.qmd) |
| Three or more treatments compared indirectly | [Network meta-analysis](network.qmd) |
| 2×2 diagnostic accuracy tables | [Diagnostic meta-analysis](diagnostic.qmd) |

Have more than one outcome to analyse? Once you have picked the module, follow
[Multiple outcomes at once](multiple-outcomes.qmd) to run them all in a single
pass.

## How to cite

If MetaVidence produced results you are publishing,
[cite MetaVidence and the analysis packages](how-to-cite.qmd). Citations are what
keep this free academic tool alive and maintained, and recording which software
produced your numbers is part of a reproducible analysis.
